+class DefinitionFrontierExtractionTests(unittest.TestCase):
+    FIXTURE = """
+namespace MIPStarRE.ComparatorDefinitionFrontierFixture
+
+def typeDependency : Type := Nat
+def registeredValueHelper : Nat := 7
+def registered (_n : typeDependency) : Nat := registeredValueHelper
+theorem ordinaryProofHelper (n : Nat) : n = n := rfl
+def ordinaryValueHelper : Nat := 1
+def ordinary : { n : Nat // n = n } :=
+  ⟨registered ordinaryValueHelper, ordinaryProofHelper _⟩
+theorem target : ordinary = ordinary := rfl
+
+end MIPStarRE.ComparatorDefinitionFrontierFixture
+"""
+
+    def _run_extractor(self, definition_names: str | None) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
+        template = (COMPARATOR / "extract_closure.lean").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
+        source = check_challenge_drift.IMPORT_BLOCK.sub(
+            "import Mathlib\n", template, count=1
+        )
+        source = source.replace(
+            "\n#eval runExtract\n",
+            "\n" + textwrap.dedent(self.FIXTURE) + "\n#eval runExtract\n",
+        )
+        with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory() as td:
+            extractor = Path(td) / "extract_fixture.lean"
+            extractor.write_text(source, encoding="utf-8")
+            env = dict(os.environ)
+            env[challenge_config.TARGETS_ENV] = (
+                "MIPStarRE.ComparatorDefinitionFrontierFixture.target"
+            )
+            env.pop(challenge_config.DEFINITIONS_ENV, None)
+            if definition_names is not None:
+                env[challenge_config.DEFINITIONS_ENV] = definition_names
+            return subprocess.run(
+                ["lake", "env", "lean", str(extractor)],
+                cwd=REPO_ROOT,
+                env=env,
+                check=False,
+                text=True,
+                stdout=subprocess.PIPE,
+                stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
+            )
+
+    @staticmethod
+    def _declaration_names(output: str) -> set[str]:
+        return {
+            line.split("\t", 1)[0]
+            for line in output.splitlines()
+            if len(line.split("\t")) in (4, 5)
+        }
+
+    def test_real_extraction_stops_only_the_registered_value(self) -> None:
+        prefix = "MIPStarRE.ComparatorDefinitionFrontierFixture."
+        selected = prefix + "registered"
+        result = self._run_extractor(selected)
+
+        self.assertEqual(result.returncode, 0, result.stdout)
+        names = self._declaration_names(result.stdout)
+        self.assertIn(selected, names)
+        self.assertIn(prefix + "typeDependency", names)
+        self.assertNotIn(prefix + "registeredValueHelper", names)
+        self.assertIn(prefix + "ordinary", names)
+        self.assertIn(prefix + "ordinaryValueHelper", names)
+        self.assertIn(prefix + "ordinaryProofHelper", names)
+        selected_row = next(

+        )

+
+        ordinary = self._run_extractor(None)
+        self.assertEqual(ordinary.returncode, 0, ordinary.stdout)
+        self.assertIn(prefix + "registeredValueHelper", self._declaration_names(ordinary.stdout))

+    def test_real_extraction_rejects_bad_registered_names(self) -> None:

1	\section{Classical and Quantum Low-degree Tests}
     2	\label{sec:ldt}
     3	
     4	In this section we introduce the classical and quantum low individual degree tests, that form the basis of our classical, quantum-sound and quantum PCP constructions. For quantum soundness of the classical test we refer to~\cite{ML20}. For the quantum test, we refer to~\cite{natarajan2018low} and its adaptation to the low individual degree test given in Appendix~\ref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
     5	The protocol in this work combines both of these tests, using the quantum
     6	low individual degree test for question reduction and the classical low individual degree test for
     7	answer reduction.
     8	Section~\ref{sec:ld-verifier} below introduces the classical test,
     9	and Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier} does the same for the quantum 
    10	test.
    11	Prior to doing this, we introduce the \emph{Magic Square game} in
    12	Section~\ref{sec:ms}, a key subroutine in the quantum test.
    13	
    14	
    15	\subsection{The classical low-degree test}
    16	\label{sec:ld-verifier}
    17	
    18	We begin with a generalization of the classical low-degree test known as the
    19	``simultaneous individual low-degree test''.
    20	We sometimes refer to this as the ``classical low-degree test'' for short.
    21	The low-degree test is used as a subroutine in the Pauli Basis test (see
    22	Section~\ref{sec:pauli-verifier}) as well as the answer-reduction normal form
    23	verifier (see Section~\ref{sec:ans}).
    24	We describe the test as a nonlocal game in Section~\ref{sec:ld-game} and show
    25	that the question distribution can be implemented as a (typed) conditionally
    26	linear distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL
    27	distributions).
    28	
    29	
    30	\subsubsection{The game}
    31	\label{sec:ld-game}
    32	
    33	The game $\game^\ld$ is parametrized by a tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
    34	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
    35	and $m$ divides $q$.
    36	We sometimes write $\game^\ld_\ldparams$ to emphasize the dependence of the
    37	classical low-degree test on the parameter tuple $\ldparams$.
    38	
    39	We first provide a high-level description of the game for $k=1$.
    40	It is based on the low-individual degree variant of the multilinearity test
    41	of~\cite{babai1991non}, where one player (called the ``points player'') receives
    42	a random point $u \in \F_q^m$, and the other player (called the ``lines
    43	player'') receives a random axis-parallel line $\line$ that contains $u$, i.e.\
    44	the line parallel to the $i$-th axis which goes through point $u$, for uniformly
    45	random $i\in\{1,\ldots,m\}$.
    46	The points player is supposed to respond with a value $a \in \F_q$, and the
    47	lines player is supposed to respond with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of
    48	degree at most $d$ such that $f_\line(u_i) = a$, where $u_i$ is the $i$-th
    49	coordinate of $u$.
    50	
    51	Suppose the players agree beforehand on a global polynomial $g: \F_q^m \to \F_q$
    52	such that every variable has degree at most $d$.
    53	Then a winning strategy is the following: the points player responds with
    54	$g(u)$, and the lines player responds with the univariate polynomial $f_\line$
    55	that is the restriction of $g$ to line $\line$; formally, for $t \in \F_q$,
    56	\[f_\line(t)=g(u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\;.\] It is easy to
    57	see that $f_\line(t)$ has degree at most $d$ in the variable $t$.
    58	Thus in this case the players will pass the low-degree test with probability
    59	$1$.
    60	The low-degree testing theorem states that the converse approximately holds: if
    61	the players pass the low-degree test with probability close to $1$, then their
    62	responses must be approximately consistent (in some sense) with a global
    63	polynomial $g$ with individual degree $d$.
    64	
    65	When $k > 1$, the players are supposed to respond with a \emph{tuple} of
    66	answers; and the test is intended to check that the players' responses are
    67	consistent with a $k$-tuple of functions $g_i: \F_q^m \to \F_q$ that are
    68	polynomials where every variable has degree at most $d$.
    69	
    70	The game that we use is slightly more elaborate than the ``axis-parallel
    71	lines-versus-points'' test just described.
    72	In addition, we have two other subtests.
    73	One is a ``diagonal line-vs-points'' test: here, the points player receives a
    74	point $u \in \F_q^m$ as before, but the lines player receives a line $\line$
    75	that goes through $u$ but is not necessarily axis-aligned.
    76	Instead, it's chosen by first picking an index $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$
    77	uniformly at random, picking $v \in \F_q^m$ uniformly at random, and letting $v'
    78	= \pi_{i-1}(v) = (0,0,\ldots,0,v_i,v_{i+1},\ldots,v_m)$ (i.e., $\pi_{i-1}$
    79	zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of its input).
    80	Then, the line is defined as the set
    81	\[
    82		\line = \{ u + tv' : t \in \F_q \}\;,
    83	\]
    84	which is a uniformly random line in the affine subspace of $\F^m_q$
    85	corresponding to all points $v$ whose first $(i-1)$ coordinates match those of
    86	$u$.
    87	The points player responds with a value $a \in \F_q$, the lines player responds
    88	with a univariate polynomial $f_\line$ of degree $md$,\footnote{Since $\line$ is
    89	  no longer axis-parallel, the restriction of an individual degree-$d$
    90	  polynomial $g$ to a line $\line$ may yield a degree $md$ polynomial.}
    91	and the verifier checks that $f_\line(t_u) = a$ (where $t_u \in \F_q$ is the
    92	projection of $u$ onto the line $\line$ with respect to a canonical
    93	parameterization of $\line$).
    94	
    95	The other additional test is a ``consistency test'', where both players receive
    96	either the same points question, the same axis-parallel lines question, or the
    97	same diagonal lines question.
    98	In all cases they are expected to respond with the same answer.
    99	
   100	
   101	
   102	\paragraph{Axis-parallel lines and diagonal lines.}
   103	Before presenting a formal description of the game $\game^\ld$, we first define
   104	what we mean by lines, and their properties.
   105	
   106	\begin{definition}[Lines]
   107	  \label{def:line}
   108		A \emph{line} $\line$ in $\F^m_q$ specified by a pair $(u,v) \in (\F_q^m)^2$
   109	  is the subset
   110	  \begin{equation}
   111	    \label{eq:line-set}
   112	    \line(u,v) = \bigl\{\, u + tv : t \in \F_q \,\bigr\} \subseteq \F_q^m \;.
   113	  \end{equation}
   114	  We call the vector $v$ a \emph{direction} of line
   115	  $\line(u,v)$.\footnote{For convenience we explicitly allow
   116	    $v=0$, in which case the line is reduced to a singleton.}
   117	  
   118	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{axis-parallel} if there is a coordinate $i \in
   119	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ for which $v$ is equal to $e_i$, the $i$-th elementary basis
   120	  vector in $\F_q^m$.
   121	  We say that such a line $\line$ is \emph{parallel to the $i$-th direction}.
   122	  A line $\line(u,v)$ is \emph{diagonal} if there exists an $i \in
   123	  \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}$ for which $v_1 = v_2 = \cdots = v_i = 0$.
   124	\end{definition}
   125	
   126	The following Proposition establishes that, for a fixed direction, a line
   127	$\line$ is an equivalence class of points on the line.
   128	\begin{proposition}
   129	  \label{prop:line-equiv}
   130	  Let $u,v \in \F_q^m$.
   131	  Then for all $u' \in \line(u,v)$, we have that $\line(u,v) = \line(u',v)$.
   132	\end{proposition}
   133	\begin{proof}
   134		Fix $u' \in \line(u,v)$.
   135	  We have that $u' = u + tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$.
   136	  Let $a \in \line(u,v)$.
   137	  This means that $a = u + sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$.
   138	  We also have that $a = u + (s - t + t)v = u + tv + (s - t)v = u' + (s - t)v$,
   139	  so $\line(u,v) \subseteq \line(u',v)$.
   140	  A similar argument shows that $\line(u',v) \subseteq \line(u,v)$.
   141	\end{proof}
   142	
   143	We now specify a canonical representation of lines $\line = \line(u,v)$ as pairs $(u_0,v)$
   144	where $u_0$ is a \emph{canonical representative} of $\line$ specified as
   145	follows.
   146	Let $L_v^{\lnf}: \F_q^m \to \F_q^m$ denote the canonical linear map with the
   147	one-dimensional kernel basis $\{v\}$ (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical} for a
   148	definition of canonical linear map).
   149	Note that for all $u \in \line$, we have that $L_v^{\lnf}(u)$ is a point in
   150	$\line$.
   151	This is because since the image and kernel of $L_v^{\lnf}$ are complementary
   152	subspaces by definition (see \Cref{def:cl-canonical}), any $u \in \F_q^m$ has a
   153	unique decomposition $u = u_0 + u_1$ where $u_0$ is in the image of $L_v^{\lnf}$
   154	and $u_1 \in \ker(L_v^{\lnf})$, which by definition is the subspace spanned by
   155	$v$.
   156	Thus $u_1 = tv$ for some $t \in \F_q$ and we have that $u_0 = u - tv \in \line$.
   157	In particular, if $u\in \line$ then $u_0 = L_v^{\lnf}(u) \in \line$ as well. 
   158	Furthermore, since $L_v^{\lnf}$ is a projection onto its image by definition, we
   159	have $L_v^{\lnf}(u_0) = u_0$.
   160	
   161	Next, note that for any $u,u' \in \line$, since $u-u' = sv$ for some $s\in \F_q$
   162	it follows that $L_v^\lnf(u) = L_v^\lnf(u')$.
   163	Thus $u_0 = u_0'$ and this shows that $L_v^\lnf$ gives a means to compute a
   164	canonical representative of lines.
   165	
   166	\begin{definition}[Canonical representative of a line]
   167	  \label{def:line-representative}
   168	  Let $\line$ be a line in direction $v$.
   169	  A canonical representative of $\line$ is the point $u_0 \in \F_q^m$ such that
   170	  \[
   171	    u_0 = L_v^\lnf(u)
   172	  \]
   173	  for all $u \in \line$.
   174	\end{definition}
   175	
   176	
   177	
   178	\paragraph{Question distribution.}
   179	We now present the question distribution of the game $\game^\ld$ as a typed CL
   180	distribution (see \Cref{sec:types} for the definition of typed CL functions and
   181	typed CL distributions).
   182	The type set $\type^\ld$ of the game $\game^\ld$ we use is
   183	\[
   184		\type^\ld = \{ \Point, \ALine, \DLine \}\;.
   185	\]
   186	The distribution over question types is uniform over $\type^\ld \times \type^\ld$.

   188	We introduce the corresponding typed CL functions $L_\Point$, $L_\ALine$,
   189	$L_\DLine$ where the corresponding CL distributions $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$
   190	and $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$ implement the axis line-versus-point and diagonal
   191	line-versus-point distributions, respectively.
   192	The functions are parametrized by a field size $q$, a dimension $m$, and three
   193	complementary register subspaces $V_\xpt,V_{\coord}, V_{\dir{}}$ of some ambient
   194	space.
   195	The register $V_\xpt$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$) is called the
   196	\emph{point register}, $V_\coord$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q$) is called the
   197	\emph{coordinate register}, and $V_{\dir{}}$ (which is isomorphic to $\F_q^m$)
   198	is called the \emph{direction register}, respectively.
   199	We let $V$ denote the direct sum $V_\xpt \oplus V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$.
   200	We identify elements of $V$ as triples $(u,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times
   201	\F_q^m$.
   202	
   203	Define $L_\Point$ to be the $1$-level CL function that projects onto $V_\xpt$: for every $(u,s,v) \in V$,
   204	\begin{equation}
   205	  \label{eq:cl-ptf}
   206		L_\Point(u,s,v) = (u,0,0) \;.
   207	\end{equation}
   208	Define $L_\ALine$ to be the following $2$-level CL function:
   209	\begin{equation}
   210	  \label{eq:cl-alnf}
   211		L_\ALine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{e_i}(u), s, 0)\ \text{for all } (u,s,v) \in V,
   212	\end{equation}
   213	where $L^\lnf$ is the linear function used to compute the canonical
   214	representative of lines (see \Cref{def:line-representative}), and $i = \chi(s)$
   215	where we define $\chi(s)$ to be the unique integer such that
   216	\begin{equation}
   217	\label{eq:chi-func}
   218		s = (\chi(s) - 1) \frac{q}{m} + r
   219	\end{equation}
   220	for some $0 \leq r < q/m$, and we interpret the field element $s \in \F_q$ as an
   221	integer between $0$ and $q - 1$).
   222	The function $L_\ALine$ is the concatenation of the $1$-level CL function that
   223	projects the subspaces $V_{\coord} \oplus V_{\dir{}}$ down to $V_\coord$ (i.e.
   224	zeroes out the entire $V_{\dir{}}$ register), and the family of $1$-level CL
   225	functions $\{L^\lnf_{e_i} \}$ acting on $V_\xpt$, indexed by $i \in
   226	\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   227	(See \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation.)
   228	Thus $L_\ALine$ is a $2$-level CL function.
   229	
   230	Define $L_\DLine$ to be the following $3$-level CL function: for all $(u,s,v) \in
   231	V$,
   232	\begin{equation}
   233	\label{eq:cl-dlnf}
   234		L_\DLine(u,s,v) = (L^\lnf_{\pi_{i-1}(v)}(u),s,\pi_{i-1}(v))
   235	\end{equation}
   236	where $i = \chi(s)$.
   237	The function $L_\DLine$ is the concatenation of the following CL functions (again, see \Cref{lem:cl-concat} for definition of CL function concatenation): (i) the identity function on $V_{\coord}$ (which is a $1$-level CL function); (ii) for every $i \in \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ the $1$-level CL function on $V_{\dir{}}$ that maps $v \mapsto \pi_{i-1}(v)$ (i.e.~it zeroes out the first $i-1$ coordinates of $v$), and (iii) for every pair $(s,v') \in V_\coord \oplus V_{\dir{}}$, the $1$-level CL function $L^\lnf_{v'}$ acting on $V_\xpt$. Thus $L_\DLine$ is a $3$-level CL function.

   240	The following two lemmas establish that the CL functions
   241	$L_\Point,L_\ALine,L_\DLine$ give rise to the axis-parallel line-versus-point and
   242	diagonal line-versus-point distributions.
   243	\begin{lemma}
   244		\label{lem:alnf}
   245		Consider the pair $(\line, u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   246	  tuple $((u_0,s,0),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$,
   247	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,e_i)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   248	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a line that
   249	  goes through $u$ and is parallel to a uniformly random axis $i \in
   250	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$.
   251	\end{lemma}
   252	\begin{proof}
   253		Since $s$ is uniformly random in $\F_q$ and $m$ divides $q$ by assumption, we
   254	  have that $i$ is uniformly random between $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ and therefore
   255	  $(u_0,s)$ specifies a uniformly random axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$.
   256	  Since $u_0 = L^{\lnf}_{e_i}(u)$, we have that $u \in \line(u_0,e_i)$.
   257	\end{proof}
   258	
   259	
   260	
   261	\begin{lemma}
   262		\label{lem:dlnf}
   263		Consider the pair $(\line,u)$ sampled in the following way: first, sample the
   264	  tuple $((u_0,s,v),(u,0,0))$ from the CL distribution $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$,
   265	  and let $\line = \line(u_0,v)$ where $i = \chi(s)$.
   266	  Then $u$ is a uniformly random point in $\F_q^m$ and $\line$ is a random
   267	  diagonal line that goes through $u$ and shares the first $i-1$ coordinates
   268	  with $u$, for uniformly random $i$.
   269	\end{lemma}
   270	\begin{proof}
   271		The proof of this follows identically to \Cref{lem:alnf}.
   272	\end{proof}

   276	\begin{definition}[Line-point distributions]
   277	        \label{def:line-point-dist}
   278	 The \emph{axis line-point distribution} $D_{\ALine}$ is the
   279	 distribution $\mu_{L_\ALine,L_\Point}$ over pairs $(\ell=(u_0,e_i),u)$
   280	 (we omit the $0$ elements for simplicity). The \emph{diagonal
   281	   line-point distribution} $D_{\DLine}$ is the distribution
   282	 $\mu_{L_\DLine,L_\Point}$  over $(\ell=(u_0,s,v),u)$. The
   283	 \emph{line-point distribution} $D_{\Line}$ is the equal mixture of the axis-parallel line-point distribution and the diagonal line-point distribution.
   284	 In other words, a sample from $D_{\Line}$ is distributed as follows:
   285	 with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\ALine}$,
   286	 and with probability $\tfrac{1}{2}$, output a sample from $D_{\DLine}$.
   287	\end{definition}

   322	The table at the top specifies a parsing scheme for the questions and answers,
   323	depending on the type of question.
   324	For example, when a player receives a question with type $\Point$, the question
   325	content $x$, a bit string of length $m \log q$, should be interpreted by the
   326	decision procedure and the players as an element of the vector space $\F_q^m$,
   327	as indicated in Section~\ref{sec:ff-representations}.
   328	Similarly the answer to a question with type $\Point$ is expected to be a bit
   329	string of length $\ldc \log q$, and is interpreted as an element of $\F_q^\ldc$.
   330	For questions with type $\ALine$, the question content is a $(m \log q + \log
   331	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a pair $(u_0, s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$,
   332	which in turn can be interpreted as a specification for an axis-parallel line
   333	$\line(u_0,e_i)$ in $\F_q^m$ where $i = \chi(s)$, as described in
   334	\Cref{lem:alnf}.
   335	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$d$ univariate
   336	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,e_i)$, each polynomial given by a
   337	list of $d+1$ coefficients.
   338	For questions with type $\DLine$, the question content is a $(2m \log q + \log
   339	q)$-bit string, which is parsed as a triple $(u_0, s, v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q
   340	\times \F_q^m$ that specifies a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ where $v' =
   341	\pi_{i-1}(v)$ as described in \Cref{lem:dlnf}.
   342	The answer is interpreted as the description of $\ldc$ degree-$md$ univariate
   343	polynomials defined on the line $\line(u_0,v')$.
   344	If the answers returned by the players do not fit this format the decision
   345	procedure rejects.

   394	We define a special class of measurements that are relevant to the soundness
   395	properties of the low-degree test.
   396	
   397	\begin{definition}[Low-degree polynomial measurements]
   398	  \label{def:ld-meas}
   399	  Define $\polymeas{m}{d}{q}$ to be the set of POVM measurements whose outcomes
   400	  correspond to (individual) degree-$d$ polynomials of $m$ variables over
   401	  $\F_q$.
   402	  More generally, for an integer $\ldc$ and tuples $m=(m_1, m_2, \ldots,
   403	  m_\ldc)$, $d=(d_1, d_2, \ldots, d_\ldc)$ and $q=(q_1, q_2, \ldots, q_\ldc)$,
   404	  we let $\simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}$ be the set of measurements $G =
   405	  \{G_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots\,,\, g_\ldc}\}$ such that for $i\in\{1, 2, \ldots,
   406	  \ldc\}$, $g_i$ is a polynomial $g_i:\F_{q_i}^{m_i} \rightarrow
   407	  \F_{q_i}$ with individual degree $d_i$ (see \Cref{sec:ld-encoding} for a definition of individual degree). 
   408	\end{definition}
   409	
   410	Quantum soundness of a version of the classical low-degree test for polynomials of low \emph{total} degree was claimed
   411	in~\cite{natarajan2018low}, building on an analysis of a three-prover version of the test in~\cite{vidick2016three}. Unfortunately there is a gap in the soundness analysis of this test. For our construction we use the low individual degree test, whose quantum soundness is shown in~\cite{ML20} and generalized in~\cite{ji2021quantum}. We state the result in the form that is most directly useful for us, and show how the stated result follows from~\cite{ji2021quantum}.
   412	
   413	\begin{theorem}[Quantum soundness of the simultaneous classical low-degree test]
   414	  \label{lem:ld-soundness}
   415	  There exists a function $\delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc) = a (dm \ldc)^a (\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})$ for universal constants $a\geq 1$ and $0<b\leq 1$ 
   416	such that the following
   417	  holds.
   418	  For all $\eps > 0$ and parameter tuple $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$, for all
   419	  projective strategies $(\psi,A,B)$ that succeed with probability at least
   420	  $1-\eps$ in the game $\game^\ld_\ldparams$, there exists measurements
   421	  \[G^w \in \simulpolymeas{m}{d}{q}{\ldc}\] on $\mH_w$, for
   422	  $w\in\{\alice,\bob\}$, such that
   423	  \begin{equation*}
   424	    \begin{split}
   425	      A^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}
   426	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   427	      G^\bob_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}\;,\\
   428	      G^\alice_{[(g_1(u),g_2(u),\ldots,g_\ldc(u)) = (a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots \,,\, a_\ldc)]}
   429	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   430				 B^{\Point,\, u}_{a_1,\, a_2,\, \ldots\,,\, a_\ldc}\;,\\
   431	      G^\alice_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}
   432	      & \abc[\delta_{\ld}]
   433	      G^\bob_{g_1,\, g_2,\, \ldots \,,\, g_\ldc}\;,
   434	    \end{split}
   435	  \end{equation*}
   436	  where $\delta_{\ld} = \delta_{\ld}(\eps, q, m, d, \ldc)$, 
   437	  and all three statements are with respect to the state $\ket{\psi}$.
   438	In addition, the first two approximations hold under the uniform distribution over $u\in \F_q^m$,
   439		whereas there is no question distribution associated with the third approximation.
   440	\end{theorem}
   441	
   442	\begin{proof}
   443	Let $\ldparams = (q, m, d, \ldc)$
   444	where $m, d, \ldc \in \N$ are integers, $q \in \N$ is an admissible field size,
   445	and $m$ divides $q$. Let $\Sigma=\F_q$. Let $\code \subseteq \Sigma^q$ be the Reed-Solomon code with degree $d$. Explicitly, $\code$ is the set of all $(p(x_1),\ldots,p(x_n))$ where $p:\F_q\to\F_q$ is a univariate polynomial of degree at most $d$ and $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ are an enumeration of $\F_q$. Then in the (standard) notation from~\cite{ji2021quantum} $\code$ is a linear $[q,d+1,n-d+1]_\Sigma$ code.
   446	
   447	Observe that the two-prover tensor code test, for the code $\code^{\otimes m}$, as described in~\cite[Figure 1 and Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}, is identical to the game $\game^\ld$ with parameters $\ldparams$ and $\ldc=1$, whose decider is presented in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider}. This is because 
   448	\begin{enumerate}
   449	\item The \emph{axis-parallel line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{axis-parallel lines test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with the only difference that in Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} the roles of A and B are chosen uniformly at random. This is consistent with the two-prover variant of the tensor code test from~\cite[Section 4.1]{ji2021quantum}.
   450	\item The \emph{diagonal line-versus-point test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{subcube commutation test} from~\cite[Figure 1]{ji2021quantum}, with again the added symmetrization between players. 
   451	\item The \emph{consistency test} from Figure~\ref{fig:ld-decider} is identical to the \emph{synchronicity test} from~\cite[Figure 2]{ji2021quantum}.
   452	\end{enumerate}
   453	
   454	As a result,~\cite[Theorem 4.7]{ji2021quantum}, in which we choose the parameter $k$ as $k=m^3d$,  immediately yields \Cref{lem:ld-soundness}.
   455	
   456	To conclude it remains to extend the result to the case of general $\ldc$. This is done 
   457	via a standard reduction, following exactly the same steps as the derivation of Theorem 4.43 from Theorem 4.40 in~\cite{NW19}.
   458	\end{proof}

  1169	    On input $(\tvar_\alice,x_\alice, \tvar_\bob, x_\bob, a_\alice, a_\bob)$,
  1170	    the decision procedure $\decider^\pauli$ performs the following checks for
  1171	    $w \in \AB$:
  1172	    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=2pt]
  1173	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1174	      \label{item:same-type}
  1175	      If $\tvar_\alice = \tvar_\bob$, accept iff $a_\alice = a_\bob$.
  1176	
  1177	    \item (\textbf{Low-degree}).
  1178	      \label{item:low-degree}
  1179	      Let $\ldparams = (q,m,d,1)$. 
  1180	      \begin{enumerate}
  1181	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\ALine, W)$, accept if
  1182	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \ALine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1183	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1184	      	\item If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\DLine, W)$, accept if
  1185	      $\decider^\ld_{\ldparams}$ accepts $(\Point, x_w, \DLine, x_{\overline{w}}, a_w,
  1186	      a_{\overline{w}})$.
  1187			\end{enumerate}
  1188	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1189	      \label{item:low-degree-consistency}
  1190	      If $\tvar_w = (\Point, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = (\Pauli, W)$, accept if
  1191	      $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}(x_w) = a_w$, where $g_{a_{\overline{w}}}$ is
  1192	      the low-degree encoding of $a_{\overline{w}} \in \F_q^M$ defined in
  1193	      Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
  1194	    \end{enumerate}
  1195	    In the remaining four cases, the decision procedure first computes the
  1196	    number
  1197	    \begin{equation}
  1198	      \label{eq:gamma-value}
  1199	      \gamma = \tr \bigl( (\ind_{m}(u_\xpt) \cdot r_\xpt) \cdot
  1200	      (\ind_{m}(u_\zpt) \cdot r_\zpt) \bigr)\;,
  1201	    \end{equation}
  1202	    where we recall the $\ind_{m}(\cdot)$ vector from Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}.
  1203	    \begin{enumerate}[itemsep=2pt,parsep=2pt]
  1204	      \setcounter{enumi}{3}
  1205	    \item (\textbf{Commutation check}).
  1206	      \label{item:commutation} If $\tvar_w = (\Pair, W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} =
  1207	      \Pair$, accept if $a_w = \beta_W$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
  1208	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1209	      \label{item:commutation-consistency} If $\tvar_w = (\Point,W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} =
  1210	      (\Pair,W)$, accept if $\tr (a_w r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}$ or $\gamma \neq 0$.
  1211	      
  1212	    \item (\textbf{Magic square check}).
  1213	      \label{item:magic-square} If $\tvar_w = \Constraint_i,
  1214	      \tvar_{\overline{w}} = \Variable_j$, accept if $\gamma = 0$, or $a_w$
  1215	      satisfies constraint $\Constraint_i$ and $ \alpha_j = a_{\overline{w}}$.
  1216	
  1217	    \item (\textbf{Consistency check}).
  1218	      \label{item:magic-square-consistency}
  1219	      If $\tvar_w = (\Point,W), \tvar_{\overline{w}} = \Variable_j$, accept if
  1220	      $\gamma = 0$ or if $j = 1$, $W = X$, and $\tr(a_w r_\xpt) =
  1221	      a_{\overline{w}}$ or if $j = 5$, $W = Z$, and $\tr(a_w r_\zpt) =
  1222	      a_{\overline{w}}$.

  1229	We describe an honest, value-$1$ PCC strategy for the Pauli basis test.
  1230	
  1231	
  1232	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:pauli-completeness}
  1233	  The Pauli basis test $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ has a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1234	\end{lemma}
  1235	
  1236	\begin{proof}
  1237	  We begin by specifying the value-$1$ strategy $\strategy = (\ket{\psi}, E)$.
  1238	  The state is
  1239	  \begin{equation*}
  1240	    \ket{\psi} = \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}\;.
  1241	  \end{equation*}
  1242	  Now we specify the measurements.
  1243	  We start with measurements associated with questions of type $\Point$,
  1244	  $\ALine$, $\DLine$, and $\Pauli$.
  1245	  Using notation introduced in Section~\ref{sec:ld-encoding}, for $W \in \{X,
  1246	  Z\}$,
  1247	  \begin{align*}
  1248	    E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{\, a}
  1249	    & = \tau^W_{[g_{\cdot}(y) = a]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1250	    E^{(\ALine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1251	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\
  1252	    E^{(\DLine,W),\, \line}_{\, f}
  1253	    & = \tau^W_{[(g_{\cdot})|_\line = f]} \otimes I\;,\\    
  1254	    E^{(\Pauli,W)}_{\, a}
  1255	    & = \tau^W_{a} \otimes I\;.
  1256	  \end{align*}
  1257	  Here, the bracket notation used to post-process measurement outcomes is
  1258	  defined in \Cref{def:bracket}.
  1259	  Thus, for example, the measurement on question $((\Point,W),y)$ corresponds to
  1260	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$, receiving an
  1261	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and then outputting the value $a = g_{h}(y)$.
  1262	
  1263	  For $\ALine$ and $\DLine$ questions, the question content $\line$ denotes
  1264	  either an axis-parallel line $\line(u_0,e_i)$ for some $i \in
  1265	  \{1,2,\ldots,m\}$, or a diagonal line $\line(u_0,v')$ for some $v' \in
  1266	  \F_q^m$.
  1267	  As described at the beginning of \Cref{sec:qld-game}, axis-parallel lines are
  1268	  specified by pairs $(u_0,s) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q$ and diagonal lines are
  1269	  specified by triples $(u_0,s,v) \in \F_q^m \times \F_q \times \F_q^m$.
  1270	  The measurement on question $((\ALine,W),\line)$, for example, corresponds to
  1271	  first performing the measurement $\{\tau^W_h\}_{h \in \F_q^M}$ to get an
  1272	  outcome $h \in \F_q^M$, and reporting the univariate polynomial $f_\line(t) =
  1273	  g_{h}(u_0 + te_i)$ where $\line$ is specified by $(u_0,s)$ and $i = \chi(s)$.
  1274	  
  1275	
  1276	
  1277	  Next we specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1278	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$.
  1279	  Questions with these question types have a question content that is a tuple
  1280	  $\omega= (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)\in (\F_q^m)^2 \times \F_q^2$.
  1281	  Given such a tuple, consider the two $\F_2$-valued POVMs $A=\{A_b\}_{b \in
  1282	    \F_2}$ and $B=\{B_b\}_{b \in \F_2}$ defined as
  1283	  \begin{align}
  1284	    A_b & = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_X)\, r_\xpt) = b]} \otimes I\;,\label{eq:gonna-expand-A}\\
  1285	    B_b & = \tau^Z_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_Z)\, r_\zpt) = b]} \otimes I\;.\label{eq:gonna-expand-B}
  1286	  \end{align}
  1287	  We would like to determine when the two observables $\mathcal{O}_A = A_0 -
  1288	  A_1$ and $\mathcal{O}_B = B_0 - B_1$ commute or anti-commute.
  1289	  Towards this we derive alternative expressions for these observables from
  1290	  which their commutativity becomes plain from inspection.
  1291	  We begin by inspecting the first matrices on the right-hand sides of
  1292	  Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B}:
  1293	  \begin{align}
  1294	  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = b]}
  1295	  &= \sum_{h : \tr(g_{h}(u_W)\, r_W) = b} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1296	  &= \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = b} \tau^W_h\;,\label{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1297	  \end{align}
  1298	  where~\eqref{eq:expand-with-dot-product}
  1299	  follows by  Definition~\ref{eq:low-degree-encoding-definition}.
  1300	  As a result,
  1301	  \begin{align}
  1302	&  \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 0]}
  1303	  -   \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(u_W)\, r_W) = 1]} \notag \\
  1304	  & = \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 0} \tau^W_h
  1305	  	- \sum_{h : \tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W ) = 1} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1306	  & = \sum_{h} (-1)^{\tr((h\, \cdot\, \ind_{m}(u_W)) \cdot r_W )} \tau^W_h\nonumber\\
  1307	  & = \tau^W(\ind_{m}(u_W)r_W)\;,\label{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1308	  \end{align}
  1309	  where the last step uses~\eqref{eq:pauli-obs-proj}.
  1310	  As a result, Equation~\eqref{eq:finally-got-an-observable}
  1311	  and Equations~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-A} and~\eqref{eq:gonna-expand-B} imply that
  1312	  \begin{equation*}
  1313	  \mathcal{O}_A = \tau^X(\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \otimes I,\quad
  1314	  \mathcal{O}_B = \tau^Z(\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z) \otimes I\;.
  1315	  \end{equation*}
  1316	  Now, let $\gamma = \tr((\ind_{m}(u_X)r_X) \cdot (\ind_{m}(u_Z)r_Z)) \in \F_2$,
  1317	  as in Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}.
  1318	  Then by Equation~\eqref{eq:twisted-fq},
  1319	  \begin{equation*}
  1320	  \mathcal{O}_A \mathcal{O}_B = (-1)^{\gamma} \mathcal{O}_B \mathcal{O}_A\;.
  1321	  \end{equation*}
  1322	  As a result, $\gamma$ quantifies whether the observables $\mathcal{O}_A$ and
  1323	  $\mathcal{O}_B$ commute, and therefore whether the measurements~$A$ and~$B$
  1324	  commute.
  1325	  If $\gamma = 0$, they commute.
  1326	  If $\gamma = 1$, they anti-commute.
  1327	  We now specify the POVMs associated with questions of type $\Constraint$,
  1328	  $\Variable$, and $\Pair$, considering separately the cases when $\gamma = 0$
  1329	  or $\gamma = 1$.
  1330	  \begin{enumerate}
  1331	  \item If $\gamma = 0$, 
  1332	     for each $\beta_X, \beta_Z \in \F_2$ define
  1333	    \begin{equation}\label{eq:pair-definition}
  1334	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{\beta_X,\, \beta_Z} = A_{\beta_X} \cdot B_{\beta_Z}\;,
  1335	    \end{equation}
  1336	    \begin{equation*}
  1337	      E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{a} = A_{a} \;,\qquad
  1338	      E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{a} = B_{a}\;.
  1339	    \end{equation*}
  1340	    The POVM associated with questions of type $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ are
  1341	    defined to be trivial.
  1342	    In particular, we define
  1343	    \begin{equation*}
  1344	      E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}_{\, 0,\, 0,\, 0}
  1345	      = E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}_{\, 0} = I\;,
  1346	    \end{equation*}
  1347	    and the remaining POVM elements in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1348	  \item If $\gamma = 1$, then $\mathcal{O}_A$ and $\mathcal{O}_B$ anti-commute.
  1349	    In this case we define measurements $E^{\Constraint_i,\, \omega}$ and
  1350	    $E^{\Variable_j,\, \omega}$, for all $i\in\{1,\ldots,6\}$ and $j
  1351	    \in\{1,\ldots,9\}$ to be those guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1352	    Measurements associated with inputs of type $\Pair$ are defined to be
  1353	    trivial.
  1354	    In particular, we define
  1355	    \begin{equation*}
  1356	      E^{\Pair,\, \omega}_{0,\, 0} = E^{(\Pair,X),\, \omega}_{0} = E^{(\Pair,Z),\, \omega}_{0} = I\;,
  1357	    \end{equation*}
  1358	    and the remaining matrices in these measurements are set to be zero.
  1359	  \end{enumerate}
  1360	  This completes the specification of the strategy.
  1361	
  1362	  Now, we show that $\strategy$ is a value-$1$ SPCC strategy.
  1363	  It is clearly symmetric and projective. 
  1364	  To show that it is consistent, we note that all measurements are Pauli basis
  1365	  measurements, which are consistent, or measurements produced by
  1366	  Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}, which are also consistent.
  1367	  The only exception is the $\Pair$ measurement in the $\gamma = 0$ case, which
  1368	  by Equation~\eqref{eq:pair-definition} is a product of two commuting,
  1369	  consistent measurements, and so it is therefore also consistent.
  1370	  To show that it is commuting, we note that for each $W \in \{X, Z\}$, all
  1371	  $(\Point, W)$, $(\ALine, W)$, $(\DLine,W)$ and $(\Pauli, W)$ measurements
  1372	  commute as they are all measurements in the Pauli~$W$ basis.
  1373	  Next, if $\gamma = 0$ then the $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ measurements
  1374	  commute trivially, and for $W \in \{X, Z\}$, the $(\Point, W)$ measurement
  1375	  commutes with the $(\Pair, W)$ measurement, as they are both $W$ basis
  1376	  measurements, and the measurement $E^{\Pair, \omega}_{\beta_X, \, \beta_Z} =
  1377	  A_{\beta_X}\cdot B_{\beta_Z}$ commutes with $E^{(\Pair, W), \omega}_{a}$
  1378	  because $A$ and~$B$ commute.
  1379	  On the other hand, if $\gamma \neq 0$, then the $\Pair$ measurements commute
  1380	  trivially, and the $\Constraint$ and $\Variable$ measurements commute by
  1381	  Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1382	  Finally, the $(\Point, X)$ measurement commutes with $\Variable_1$ because
  1383	  both are $X$-basis measurements, and likewise both $(\Point, Z)$ and
  1384	  $\Variable_5$ are $Z$-basis measurements.
  1385	  
  1386	  It remains to show that $\strategy$ is value-$1$.
  1387		Consider first the first three tests executed by the decision procedure in
  1388	  Figure~\ref{fig:decider_pauli}.
  1389	  The strategy passes the consistency checks with probability~$1$ because it is
  1390	  projective and consistent.
  1391	  It passes the low-degree checks because it answers those consistently with an
  1392	  honest strategy in the classical low-degree test.
  1393			
  1394	  Next, consider the remaining four tests.
  1395	  Fix an $\omega= (u_\xpt, u_\zpt, r_\xpt, r_\zpt)$ and~$\gamma$ as
  1396	  in~\eqref{eq:gamma-value}.
  1397	  If $\gamma = 0$, then the strategy passes the commutation check with
  1398	  probability~$1$ by construction.
  1399	  As for the consistency check in Item~\ref{item:commutation-consistency},
  1400	  we can write the $(\Point, W)$ measurement as follows: 
  1401	  \begin{equation*}
  1402	  E^{(\Point,W),\, y}_{[\tr(\,\cdot\, r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]}
  1403	  = \tau^W_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(y)r_W) = a_{\overline{w}}]} \otimes I
  1404	  = E^{(\Pair, W), \omega}_{a_{\overline{w}}} \otimes I.
  1405	  \end{equation*}
  1406	  As a result, due to the consistency of the $(\Pair, W)$ measurement, the
  1407	  consistency check is passed with probability~$1$.
  1408	  On the other hand, if $\gamma \neq 0$, then the strategy passes the Magic
  1409	  Square check by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1410	  As for the consistency check in Item~\ref{item:magic-square-consistency}, we
  1411	  can write the $(\Point, X)$ measurement as follows:
  1412	  \begin{equation*}
  1413	  E^{(\Point,X),\, y}_{[\tr(\,\cdot\, r_X) = a_{\overline{w}}]}
  1414	  = \tau^X_{[\tr(g_{\cdot}(y)r_X) = a_{\overline{w}}]} \otimes I
  1415	  = E^{\Variable_1,\, \omega}_{a_{\overline{w}}} \otimes I,
  1416	  \end{equation*}
  1417	  where the last step is by Theorem~\ref{thm:ms-from-ac}.
  1418	  As these measurements are consistent, this test is passed with
  1419	  probability~$1$.
  1420	\end{proof}

  1426	\paragraph{Soundness of the Pauli basis test.} 
  1427	We state the soundness properties of the Pauli basis test.
  1428	The following is an adaptation of the self-testing statement in~\cite[Theorem
  1429	6.4]{NW19}.
  1430	
  1431	\begin{theorem}
  1432	  \label{thm:pauli}
  1433	There exists a function 
  1434	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1435	 for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeed with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^q)^{\otimes M}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1436	\begin{enumerate}
  1437	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1438	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1439	    \begin{gather*}
  1440	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\tau^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1441	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\tau^W_u)_{\bob''}\;,
  1442	    \end{gather*}
  1443	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$.
  1444	\end{enumerate}
  1445	\end{theorem}
  1446	
  1447	We provide a proof of \Cref{thm:pauli} in \Cref{sec:qld-analysis}. 
  1448	
  1449	
  1450	The strategies described in the proof of \Cref{lem:pauli-completeness} and in the conclusion of \Cref{thm:pauli} are described in terms of qudit Pauli measurements and maximally entangled states defined over $q$-dimensional qudits. 
  1451	However, it is more convenient for our application of the Pauli basis test to
  1452	instead deal with \emph{qubits}.
  1453	In particular, we use the Pauli basis test in the ``introspection game'' of
  1454	Section~\ref{sec:introspection}, where the players are commanded to sample
  1455	questions according to a sampler $\sampler$ of a normal form verifier.
  1456	By definition of normal form verifier, $\sampler$ is a sampler over $\F_2$, and
  1457	therefore it is natural to use a test for qubit Pauli measurements.
  1458	
  1459	Since we use field sizes $q$ that are powers of $2$, Lemma~\ref{lem:pauli-binary}
  1460	shows that the conclusions of \Cref{thm:pauli} can also be described in terms of
  1461	testing for maximally entangled states over qubits and qubit Pauli measurements.

  1469	\begin{corollary}
  1470	\label{cor:pauli-binary}  
  1471	There exists a function
  1472	\[\delta_{\qld}(\eps,q,m,d) = a(md)^a(\eps^b + q^{-b} + 2^{-bmd})\]
  1473	for universal constants $a \geq 1$ and $0 < b < 1$ such that the following holds. For all admissible parameter tuples $\qldparams = (q,m,d)$ and for all strategies $\strategy = (\ket{\psi},A,B)$ for the game $\game^\pauli_\qldparams$ that succeeds with probability at least $1 - \eps$, there exist local isometries $\phi_\alice: \mH_\alice \to \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\alice''},\phi_\bob: \mH_\bob \to \mH_{\bob'} \otimes \mH_{\bob''}$ (where $\ket{\psi} \in \mH_\alice \otimes \mH_\bob$ and $\mH_{\alice''},\mH_{\bob''} \cong (\C^2)^{\otimes M \log q}$ with $M = 2^m$) and a state $\ket{\aux} \in \mH_{\alice'} \otimes \mH_{\bob'}$ such that 
  1474	\begin{enumerate}
  1475	    \item $\left \| \phi_\alice \otimes \phi_B \ket{\psi} - \ket{\aux} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes M \log q}  \right \| \leq \delta_{\qld}(\eps,m,d,q)$,
  1476	    \item Letting $\tilde{A}^x_a = \phi_A\, A^x_a \, \phi_A^\dagger$ and $\tilde{B}^y_b = \phi_B B^y_b \phi_B^\dagger$, we have for $W \in \{X,Z\}$
  1477	    \begin{gather*}
  1478	        \tilde{A}^{(\pauli,W)}_u \otimes I_{\bob'\bob''} \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} (\sigma^W_u)_{\alice''} \otimes I_{\alice' \bob' \bob''} \\
  1479	        I_{\alice'\alice''} \otimes \tilde{B}^{(\pauli,W)}_u    \approx_{\delta_{\qld}} I_{\alice' \alice'' \bob'} \otimes (\sigma^W_u)_{\bob''}
  1480	    \end{gather*}
  1481	    where the $\approx_{\delta_{\qld}}$ statement holds with respect to the state $\ket{\aux}_{\alice'\bob'} \otimes \ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes M \log q}_{\alice''\bob''}$ and the answer summation is over $u \in \F_q^M$. Here, $\sigma^W_u$ denotes the tensor product of single-qubit Pauli measurements
  1482	    \[
  1483	    	\bigotimes_{i=1}^{M} \bigotimes_{j=1}^{\log q} \sigma^W_{u_{ij}}
  1484	    \]
  1485	    where $\kappa(u_i) = (u_{ij})_{1 \leq j \leq \log q}$ (using the bijection $\kappa: \F_q \to \F_2^{\log q}$ from \Cref{sec:finite-fields}).
  1486	\end{enumerate}  
  1487	\end{corollary}
  1488	
  1489	\begin{proof}
  1490	\Cref{lem:pauli-binary} implies that there are local isometries that map $\ket{\EPR_q}^{\otimes M}$ to $\ket{\EPR_2}^{\otimes M\log q}$, and map the generalized Pauli measurements $\tau^W_u$ to $\bigotimes_{i=1}^M \bigotimes_{j=1}^{\log q} \sigma^W_{u_{ij}}$ where $\kappa(u_i) = (u_{i1},\ldots,u_{i\log q})$. Combining this with the isometries guaranteed by \Cref{thm:pauli}, we obtain the statement of the Corollary.
  1491	\end{proof}
  1492	\subsubsection{Canonical parameters and complexity of the Pauli basis test}
  1493	\label{sec:qld-complexity}
  1494	
  1495	We specify a canonical setting of the parameter tuple $\qldparams$ as a function

  1504	  \label{def:introparams}

  1506	  Let $c$ denote the smallest even integer that is at least $(b + a)/b$.
  1507	  For all integers $R \geq 4$, define the tuple $\introparams(R) = (q,m,d)$
  1508	  where
  1509	  \begin{itemize}
  1510	  	\item $q = 2^k$ for $k = c \lceil  \log \log R  \rceil + 1$.

     6	# Exact bridges for compact Pauli extraction quantities
     7	
     8	This module identifies the compact Pauli parameter record, prescribed-answer
     9	effects, ideal projectors, witnesses, and extraction errors with the registered
    10	QPBT definitions.  Every comparison is an equality; no quantitative estimate
    11	or soundness assumption is introduced here.
    12	
    13	The legacy import form is required because the registered soundness modules
    14	have not yet been converted to Lean's module system.
    15	
    16	## References
    17	
    18	`references/qpbt-paper/04_preliminaries.tex:1052-1208`;
    19	`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:1229-1491`.
    20	-/

    84	/-- The concrete compact SPCC predicate is exactly the transported symmetric-game predicate. -/
    85	theorem isPauliSPCC_iff_isSPCC (P : MIPStarRE.QPBT.AdmissibleParams)
    86	    (S : SymmetricPauliStrategy (PauliParams.ofAdmissibleParams P)
    87	      (MIPStarRE.QPBT.PauliScalar P)) :
    88	    S.IsPauliSPCC (PauliParams.ofAdmissibleParams P)
    89	        (MIPStarRE.QPBT.binaryRepresentation P.model) ↔
    90	      S.IsSPCC (pauliSymmetricGame P) := by
    91	  unfold SymmetricStrategy.IsPauliSPCC SymmetricStrategy.IsSPCC
    92	  have hgame := congrArg Game.μ
    93	    (pauliSymmetricGame_toGame P)
    94	  have hmu : (pauliSymmetricGame P).μ =
    95	      pauliQuestionPMF (PauliParams.ofAdmissibleParams P)
    96	        (MIPStarRE.QPBT.binaryRepresentation P.model) := by
    97	    simpa only [pauliGame] using hgame

conditionally-linear question sampler, and the Boolean win predicate for the
Pauli basis test.  The quantitative soundness theorem is isolated in

self-dual-normal identification is not quantified in the test statement.  This
is blueprint
`def:admissible`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/
structure AdmissibleParams where
  q : ℕ
  m : ℕ
  d : ℕ
  hd : 1 ≤ d
  hq : IsAdmissibleSize q
  hdvd : m ∣ q

/-- Every admissible parameter tuple has positive ambient dimension. This
follows from positivity of the admissible field size and the divisibility
`P.m ∣ P.q` in `def:admissible`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/
theorem AdmissibleParams.one_le_m (P : AdmissibleParams) : 1 ≤ P.m := by
  have hqpos : 0 < P.q := by
    rcases P.hq with ⟨k, _, hq⟩
    rw [hq]
    exact Nat.pow_pos (by decide)

compatibility view of the global `fixedFieldModel` selector, not an independently
quantified field representation.  This is the field representation of
`def:admissible`, blueprint `ch13_qpbt_test.tex`; paper
origin `references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/
@[reducible] noncomputable def AdmissibleParams.model
    (P : AdmissibleParams) : FixedFieldModel P.q :=
  fixedFieldModel P.q P.hq

tuple.  It is not an additional hypothesis of `thm:pauli`.  The low-degree
parameters are those of `def:ld-game`, blueprint
`blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex`, paper origin
`references/qpbt-paper/08_classical_and_quantum_low_degree_tests.tex:958-961`.
-/

  q := P.q
  m := P.m
  d := P.d

  hm := P.one_le_m
  hd := P.hd

  hq := P.hq
  hdvd := P.hdvd

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:252:	The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.

blueprint/src/chapter/ch13_qpbt_test.tex:1152:	The linked declaration states the theorem above, over an arbitrary strategy of the Magic Square game with the two consistency defects bounded by $\delta$, and it is proved. The formal proof splits at $\sqrt\eps + \sqrt\delta \ge 1$, where the seven conclusions hold for the trivial witness; in the complementary regime the witness is the tensor of the two players' two-qubit controlled-swap embeddings, composed with the dilation embedding. Each of those embeddings composes two one-qubit controlled swaps, one for each of two logical pairs of that player's $\pm 1$ reflections on the dilated state, and the two players' pairs are not chosen symmetrically. Bob's are his variable reflections at the cells of $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$ and at those of $\mathsf{Variable}_2$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_4$. Alice's first pair is her variable reflections at the cells of $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$, but her second is her \emph{constraint} reflections at the cells of $\mathsf{Variable}_2$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_4$, read from the first and from the second row. That asymmetry is forced by the hypothesis: \eqref{eq:ms-rigidity-consistency} compares the two players only at $\mathsf{Variable}_1$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_5$, so their $\mathsf{Variable}_2$ and $\mathsf{Variable}_4$ measurements cannot be compared, whereas Alice's constraint reflections at those two cells are compared with Bob's variable reflections there by a question pair that the distribution does sample. Item~1 is the joint state estimate on the dilation, which needs the approximate anticommutation of both of Alice's pairs, the cross-player agreement of all four pairs of corresponding reflections, and the approximate commutation of the two pairs of each player; the anticommutation of the second pair comes from a second closed path through the grid, which crosses the exceptional third column once and therefore returns the reversed product with the opposite sign. The bit-measurement relations come from the transport of the first logical pair through those embeddings, exactly for the phase observable and up to the anticommutator defect of that pair for the shift observable; the anticommutation consequences come from the solution-group computation on the dilation, products composing under conjugation by an isometry. Every conclusion is then moved from the dilated strategy to the original one by the leakage bounds of the dilation, with an explicit universal constant, which the formalization takes to be $2 \cdot 10^{12}$. The specialization to symmetric consistent strategies ($\delta = 0$) is stated as a separate declaration derived from it.

   232		Fix $\mathsf{ldparams} = (q,m,d,k)$. Answers in the game $\mathfrak{G}^{\mathrm{ld}}_{\mathsf{ldparams}}$ take the following forms, depending on the question type; answers not of the prescribed form are rejected.
   233		\begin{itemize}

   251	\begin{remark}[Diagonal questions with zero direction]\label{rem:ld-win-zero-direction}
   252		The source states the two line-versus-point clauses with ``the'' $t \in \F_q$ such that $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v$. When the direction is nonzero and $x_{\overline w}$ lies on the line, exactly one such $t$ exists and the formulation above agrees with the source. But zero directions occur: Definition~\ref{def:line} explicitly permits them, and the question distribution of Definition~\ref{def:ld-question-distribution} produces $\mathsf{DLine}$ questions with $v' = \pi_{i-1}(v) = 0$ with positive probability, namely whenever the last $m - i + 1$ coordinates of $v$ vanish. In that case $\ell(u_0, 0) = \{u_0\}$, every $t \in \F_q$ satisfies $x_{\overline w} = u_0 + t v'$ when $x_{\overline w} = u_0$, and the source clause does not determine acceptance for a nonconstant answer polynomial. The universal quantification over $t$ adopted in Definition~\ref{def:ld-win-predicate} makes the predicate a well-defined function of its arguments; it accepts vacuously when no such $t$ exists, a case the question distribution never produces. Completeness is unaffected: the restriction of a polynomial $g$ to the singleton line $\ell(u_0,0)$, expressed through the parameterization $t \mapsto u_0 + t \cdot 0$, is the constant polynomial with value $g(u_0)$, which passes the check for every $t$. Soundness is likewise unaffected: zero directions occur with probability at most $2/(mq)$, so any acceptance convention on this event changes success probabilities by at most that amount; the game-correspondence obligation enumerated in the proof of Theorem~\ref{lem:ld-soundness} accounts for this event explicitly, and an error of this shape is absorbed into the universal constants of $\delta_{\mathrm{ld}}$.
   253	\end{remark}

     6	Pauli basis test,
     7	[QPBT-comparator](https://github.com/Dengnifer/QPBT-comparator) — to verify,
     8	with the official
     9	[leanprover/comparator](https://github.com/leanprover/comparator), that this
    10	library proves the target theorems.  Background and trust model:
    11	`docs/comparator.md`.
    12	
    13	A generated challenge imports only Mathlib and, when split, its own mirror
    14	modules.  It re-declares, verbatim and in dependency order, every declaration
    15	in the kernel closure of its target statements.  Per-declaration provenance
    16	comments are included by default; a size-constrained configuration may omit
    17	them without changing the declaration text.  The targets themselves are stated
    18	with `sorry`.
    19	
    20	## Challenges
    21	
    22	Each challenge is one configuration file under `challenges/`:
    23	
    24	| file | targets | expected copy | challenge repository |
    25	|---|---|---|---|
    26	| `challenges/ldt.json` | `MIPStarRE.LDT.Test.mainFormal` | `expected/Challenge.lean.expected` | [LDT-comparator](https://github.com/LionSR/LDT-comparator) |
    27	| `challenges/qpbt.json` | four QPBT headline theorems | `expected/qpbt/` (one module per library module) | [QPBT-comparator](https://github.com/Dengnifer/QPBT-comparator) |
    28	| `challenges/palomar.json` | four compact Palomar aliases | `expected/palomar/Challenge.lean.expected` | Palomar prototype |
    29	
    30	The four QPBT targets are `MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_spcc_value_one`,
    31	`MIPStarRE.QPBT.exists_ld_soundness`, `MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness`, and
    32	`MIPStarRE.QPBT.pauli_soundness_qubit`.
    33	
    34	The Palomar targets are the corresponding compact aliases under
    35	`MIPStarRE.QPBT.Palomar`.  Its configuration registers exactly
    36	`MIPStarRE.QPBT.fixedFieldModel` as a named-definition value frontier and sets
    37	`provenance_comments` to `false`; all declaration source remains verbatim, but
    38	the repeated source-range lines do not consume the single-file line budget.
    39	
    40	A configuration names the Lean modules the extractor imports, the target
    41	theorems whose statement closure it takes, the header and footer files wrapped
    42	around the assembled body, the checked-in expected copy, and the per-challenge
    43	elaboration-context tables (`extras`, `module_preludes`).  The schema, with the
    44	meaning of every key, is documented at the top of `challenge_config.py`; unknown
    45	keys are rejected, so a typo fails loudly rather than silently dropping context.
    46	
    47	### Registered definition frontiers
    48	
    49	The optional `definition_names` list implements the official comparator's
    50	named-definition frontier.  Each registered name must resolve to a
    51	repository-local definition.  Its full type and every dependency of that type
    52	remain in the extracted closure, but its value is not traversed.  Every
    53	unregistered definition value and theorem proof reached by the ordinary closure
    54	is still traversed.
    55	
    56	The assembler copies the registered declaration's source header, preserving its
    57	name, universe parameters, binders, return type, and safety modifier, and
    58	replaces only its generated Challenge value with `by sorry`.  Missing names and
    59	names that are not definitions fail extraction.  The fifth closure-TSV column
    60	records the definition safety checked from Lean metadata.
    61	
    62	This Challenge hole is not a permission for an unchecked Solution axiom.  The
    63	official comparator compares the registered definition's name, universes, type,
    64	and safety while deliberately ignoring its Challenge value.  It separately
    65	traverses the actual Solution definition value during the Solution axiom audit.
    66	Thus the generated Challenge may contain `sorryAx` at the registered value, but
    67	the checked Solution must still supply an implementation using only the
    68	permitted axioms.  Registering one definition does not erase unrelated helper
    69	proofs or values.  `MIPStarRE/QPBT/Test/AxiomAudit.lean` checks the actual
    70	`fixedFieldModel` value transitively and currently requires exactly the same
    71	three standard Lean axioms as the four theorem aliases.
    72	
    73	The historical LDT and QPBT challenges do not set `definition_names`; omitting
    74	it or setting it to `[]` preserves their extraction and golden fixtures
    75	byte-for-byte.  The compact Palomar challenge registers only
    76	`MIPStarRE.QPBT.fixedFieldModel`.
    77

    79

    24	/-- Relabel the outcomes of a compact POVM along an equivalence. -/

    26	    [DecidableEq I] (e : A ≃ B) (M : POVM A I) : POVM B I where

    28	  pos := fun b => M.pos (e.symm b)
    29	  sum_eq_one := by
    30	    calc
    31	      ∑ b : B, M.effect (e.symm b) = ∑ a : A, M.effect a :=

    30	/-- Pushing a PMF through an equivalence preserves its mass at corresponding points. -/
    31	@[simp] theorem map_equiv_apply {X Y : Type*} (p : PMF X) (e : X ≃ Y) (x : X) :
    32	    (p.map e) (e x) = p x := by
    33	  classical
    34	  simp [PMF.map_apply, e.injective.eq_iff]
    35	
    36	/-- A PMF pushed through an equivalence is evaluated by pulling the point back. -/
    37	theorem map_equiv_apply' {X Y : Type*} (p : PMF X) (e : X ≃ Y) (y : Y) :
    38	    (p.map e) y = p (e.symm y) := by
    39	  simpa only [e.apply_symm_apply] using map_equiv_apply p e (e.symm y)
    40	
    41	end PMF

    45	/-- Outcome relabeling preserves state-dependent consistency exactly. -/
    46	theorem relabel_isConsistentOn_iff {A B I : Type*} [Fintype A] [Fintype B]
    47	    [Fintype I] [DecidableEq A] [DecidableEq B] [DecidableEq I]
    48	    (e : A ≃ B) (M : POVM A I) (ψ : EuclideanSpace ℂ (I × I)) :
    49	    (relabel e M).IsConsistentOn ψ ↔ M.IsConsistentOn ψ := by
    50	  constructor
    51	  · intro h a
    52	    simpa using h (e a)
    53	  · intro h b
    54	    exact h (e.symm b)
    55	
    56	end POVM

    58	/-- Positive-support commutation is invariant under exact question and outcome relabeling. -/
    59	theorem isCommutingOn_relabel_iff
    60	    {X Y A B X' Y' A' B' I : Type*}
    61	    [Fintype X] [Fintype Y] [Fintype A] [Fintype B]
    62	    [Fintype X'] [Fintype Y'] [Fintype A'] [Fintype B']
    63	    [Fintype I] [DecidableEq I]
    64	    (μ : PMF (X × Y)) (alice : X → POVM A I) (bob : Y → POVM B I)
    65	    (eX : X ≃ X') (eY : Y ≃ Y') (eA : A ≃ A') (eB : B ≃ B') :
    66	    IsCommutingOn (μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY))
    67	        (fun x => POVM.relabel eA (alice (eX.symm x)))
    68	        (fun y => POVM.relabel eB (bob (eY.symm y))) ↔
    69	      IsCommutingOn μ alice bob := by
    70	  constructor
    71	  · intro h x y hxy a b
    72	    have hxy' : 0 < (μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY)) (eX x, eY y) := by
    73	      rw [show (eX x, eY y) = (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY) (x, y) by rfl]
    74	      simpa only [PMF.map_equiv_apply] using hxy
    75	    simpa using h (eX x) (eY y) hxy' (eA a) (eB b)
    76	  · intro h x y hxy a b
    77	    have hxy' : 0 < μ (eX.symm x, eY.symm y) := by
    78	      rw [PMF.map_equiv_apply'] at hxy
    79	      simpa using hxy
    80	    simpa using h (eX.symm x) (eY.symm y) hxy' (eA.symm a) (eB.symm b)
    81

    84	/-- Relabeling a compact game and then relabeling by the inverse equivalences is exact. -/
    85	theorem relabel_symm_relabel {X Y A B X' Y' A' B' : Type}
    86	    [Fintype X] [Fintype Y] [Fintype A] [Fintype B]
    87	    [Fintype X'] [Fintype Y'] [Fintype A'] [Fintype B']
    88	    [DecidableEq X] [DecidableEq Y] [DecidableEq A] [DecidableEq B]
    89	    [DecidableEq X'] [DecidableEq Y'] [DecidableEq A'] [DecidableEq B']
    90	    (G : Game X Y A B) (eX : X ≃ X') (eY : Y ≃ Y')
    91	    (eA : A ≃ A') (eB : B ≃ B') :
    92	    Game.relabel (Game.relabel G eX eY eA eB)
    93	        eX.symm eY.symm eA.symm eB.symm = G := by
    94	  apply Game.ext
    95	  · ext xy
    96	    change ((G.μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY)).map
    97	      (Equiv.prodCongr eX.symm eY.symm)) xy = G.μ xy
    98	    rw [PMF.map_equiv_apply']
    99	    change (G.μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY))
   100	      ((Equiv.prodCongr eX eY) xy) = G.μ xy
   101	    exact PMF.map_equiv_apply G.μ (Equiv.prodCongr eX eY) xy
   102	  · funext x y a b
   103	    simp [Game.relabel]
   104	
   105	end Game

   109	/-- Relabel the questions and answers of a compact symmetric game. -/
   110	def relabel {X A X' A' : Type}
   111	    [Fintype X] [Fintype A] [Fintype X'] [Fintype A']
   112	    [DecidableEq X] [DecidableEq A] [DecidableEq X'] [DecidableEq A']
   113	    (G : SymmetricGame X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A') :
   114	    SymmetricGame X' A' where
   115	  toGame := Game.relabel G.toGame eX eX eA eA
   116	  μ_symm := by
   117	    intro x y
   118	    change (G.μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eX)) (x, y) =
   119	      (G.μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eX)) (y, x)
   120	    rw [PMF.map_equiv_apply', PMF.map_equiv_apply']
   121	    exact G.μ_symm (eX.symm x) (eX.symm y)
   122	  decide_symm := by
   123	    intro x y a b
   124	    exact G.decide_symm (eX.symm x) (eX.symm y) (eA.symm a) (eA.symm b)
   125	
   126	end SymmetricGame

   133	    (S : SymmetricStrategy X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A') :

   141	/-- Symmetric relabeling agrees with relabeling the underlying general strategy. -/
   142	@[simp] theorem relabel_toStrategy {X A X' A' : Type}
   143	    [Fintype X] [Fintype A] [Fintype X'] [Fintype A']
   144	    (S : SymmetricStrategy X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A') :

   149	/-- Symmetric relabeling preserves projectivity of the measurement family exactly. -/
   150	theorem relabel_isProjective_iff {X A X' A' : Type}
   151	    [Fintype X] [Fintype A] [Fintype X'] [Fintype A']
   152	    (S : SymmetricStrategy X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A') :
   153	    (∀ x, ((relabel S eX eA).meas x).IsProjective) ↔
   154	      ∀ x, (S.meas x).IsProjective := by
   155	  constructor
   156	  · intro h x
   157	    have hx := h (eX x)
   158	    change (POVM.relabel eA (S.meas (eX.symm (eX x)))).IsProjective at hx
   159	    rw [eX.symm_apply_apply] at hx
   160	    exact (POVM.relabel_isProjective_iff eA (S.meas x)).mp hx
   161	  · intro h x
   162	    exact (POVM.relabel_isProjective_iff eA (S.meas (eX.symm x))).mpr
   163	      (h (eX.symm x))

   165	/-- Symmetric relabeling preserves consistency exactly. -/
   166	theorem relabel_isConsistent_iff {X A X' A' : Type}
   167	    [Fintype X] [Fintype A] [Fintype X'] [Fintype A']
   168	    [DecidableEq A] [DecidableEq A']
   169	    (S : SymmetricStrategy X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A') :
   170	    (relabel S eX eA).IsConsistent ↔ S.IsConsistent := by
   171	  constructor
   172	  · intro h x
   173	    have hx := h (eX x)
   174	    change (POVM.relabel eA (S.meas (eX.symm (eX x)))).IsConsistentOn S.ψ at hx
   175	    rw [eX.symm_apply_apply] at hx
   176	    exact (POVM.relabel_isConsistentOn_iff eA (S.meas x) S.ψ).mp hx
   177	  · intro h x
   178	    exact (POVM.relabel_isConsistentOn_iff eA (S.meas (eX.symm x)) S.ψ).mpr
   179	      (h (eX.symm x))
   180	
   181	/-- Symmetric relabeling preserves the SPCC predicate under the exact PMF push-forward. -/
   182	theorem relabel_isSPCC_iff {X A X' A' : Type}
   183	    [Fintype X] [Fintype A] [Fintype X'] [Fintype A']
   184	    [DecidableEq X] [DecidableEq A] [DecidableEq X'] [DecidableEq A']
   185	    (G : SymmetricGame X A) (G' : SymmetricGame X' A')
   186	    (S : SymmetricStrategy X A) (eX : X ≃ X') (eA : A ≃ A')
   187	    (hμ : G.μ.map (Equiv.prodCongr eX eX) = G'.μ) :
   188	    (relabel S eX eA).IsSPCC G' ↔ S.IsSPCC G := by
   189	  rw [SymmetricStrategy.IsSPCC, SymmetricStrategy.IsSPCC, ← hμ]
   190	  constructor
   191	  · rintro ⟨hproj, hcons, hcomm⟩
   192	    exact ⟨(relabel_isProjective_iff S eX eA).mp hproj,
   193	      (relabel_isConsistent_iff S eX eA).mp hcons,
   194	      (isCommutingOn_relabel_iff G.μ S.meas S.meas eX eX eA eA).mp hcomm⟩
   195	  · rintro ⟨hproj, hcons, hcomm⟩
   196	    exact ⟨(relabel_isProjective_iff S eX eA).mpr hproj,
   197	      (relabel_isConsistent_iff S eX eA).mpr hcons,
   198	      (isCommutingOn_relabel_iff G.μ S.meas S.meas eX eX eA eA).mpr hcomm⟩
   199	
   200	end SymmetricStrategy
